who: Ordinary men and women of Varrock, Misthalin's capital: people crossing the square on errands, shopping at the stalls, queuing for tea or heading home past the palace. They live with the king up the road, the Grand Exchange next door and armed adventurers in every street, so they've seen every sort and are hard to impress, but they still love a bit of gossip.
notices: whether you look like trouble: a weapon out, far too much armour for a trip to the shops, or the look of the muggers and thieves round the south gate
what you've got on, measured against what Horvik, Lowe and Thessalia sell in the square
money: flash gear the pickpockets will be after, or someone who looks too skint to buy a cup of tea
whether you're in their way when they're in a hurry
the state of you: hurt, out of breath, bald in the wind, or starkers in a public street
your pet, and whether it's going to bother the fur stall, the tea stall or somebody's cat
values: getting on with their own business without adventurers under their feet
knowing what a thing costs, and not being overcharged for it
a quiet life with no demons at the stone circle, no zombies and no bandits in the square
their city being the biggest and best, ahead of Falador and certainly ahead of Lumbridge
a cup of tea and a sit down
news and gossip: what the Herald says, what's going on at the palace, who's sighing in the square
measuresBy: what it would fetch at the Grand Exchange
a cup of tea from the stall by the east bank
the dark wizards on the Lumbridge road
Lumbridge, where the brand-new adventurers come from
address: Usually nothing at all, or 'traveller' or 'adventurer' when they need to call you something. 'Guv' turns up now and then from street sorts (the paper seller, someone after your money, someone being cheeky), never more than once in a line and not in most lines.

nativeWords.use: street-level 'sir' for a customer or someone you want something from, usually at the end of a sentence; cheeky, never servile
nativeWords.evidence: Transcript:Benny ('Certainly, Guv. That'll be 50 coins, please.'); Transcript:Charlie the Tramp ('Spare some change, guv?'); TONE.md lists it for Varrock street folk

grammar: plain, complete sentences with ordinary contractions: it's, you'll, I'd
British tag questions and hedges: isn't it?, didn't you?, I expect, I shouldn't wonder
news comes as hearsay: They say..., I hear..., Word is..., The Herald says...
muttered remarks drop the subject: 'Looks like rain.' 'Must save you a fortune on combs.'
places and shops named exactly and locally: the square, the east bank, Horvik's, the Blue Moon
rhythm: Mostly one sentence, said in passing by someone with somewhere to be. Now and then a question at you, a grumble that trails off, or a quick exclamation. It lands on a sensible, slightly peevish reaction, not a set-up and punchline.
taboos: no swearing, modern slang or anything from our world
never names a quest, and never gives a number about the player
doesn't gush; praise is understated ('Very smart, that.', 'Fair play.')
doesn't claim inside knowledge of the palace, the gangs or the Mahjarrat; at most it's hearsay
no 'love', 'pet', 'duck' or 'mate'; 'guv' at most once in a line, and only in some lines
doesn't pretend to have been to Varlamore or Morytania; that's all from the Herald or the Blue Moon

avoid: music-hall Cockney: dropped h's, rhyming slang, 'cor blimey guv'nor', 'innit'
Dickensian urchin patter from grown adults
the old 'gypsy' label for Aris; she's a fortune-teller
cartoon city snobbery about Lumbridge or Falador; it's mild city pride, not contempt
treating the guards as villains; to locals they're bored and overworked
anything that sounds like our London: the Tube, real pub names, football, the City
